after: ## Three things to analyse in every source
alt: Three cards: content (what the source says and shows), provenance (who made it, when, why and for whom) and context (what was happening and what you know). Below, a chain: content shows a view, provenance explains why, context shows how it fits.
caption: Content, provenance and context: connect all three.

alt: Six steps for reading a cartoon, in order: caption and labels, figures and caricature, symbols, action, the message in one sentence, and provenance, which can explain why two cartoons of the same event disagree.
caption: Work from labels and symbols to the message, then use provenance to explain it.

alt: Question 1 frame: an example question on the Munich Agreement, then two details from the source, one supported by contextual knowledge and one by provenance.
caption: Two explained details, one backed by context and one by provenance.

after: ## Question 2: how useful are two sources? (12 marks)
alt: Three steps for each source in question 2: content and context, provenance, and what it is less useful for. Below, a table of what different source types are useful evidence of, including a Soviet newspaper on Hungary in 1956.
caption: Every source is useful for something: the skill is saying what for.

after: ## Worked example: BD Conflict and tension in Asia
alt: Vertical timeline: Inchon landings in September 1950 and the advance towards the Yalu, Chinese intervention in October 1950, MacArthur's call for attacks on China, retreat below the 38th parallel in winter 1950-51, and his dismissal in April 1951.
caption: The contextual knowledge that makes Sources B and C useful.

after: ## Worked example: BD Conflict and tension in Asia
alt: Table evaluating two invented sources on MacArthur's dismissal by content, context, provenance and limits: a British cartoon of April 1951 and an American soldier's letter of January 1951. A note shows they are most useful together.
caption: Evaluate each source on content, context and provenance, then combine them.

alt: Time bar: about five minutes for question 1 and fifteen for question 2. Annotate each source by circling the date and author, underlining two content details and noting one fact. Write one paragraph per source and a comparing sentence.
